title: Owner can drain accumulated sUSDS/BPT via rescueERC20 / withdrawBPT, and can unilaterally redirect future donation USDC via setBatchMinter; combined this is plenary control over all dispatched yield
description:
The owner role on BalancerPoolerV2 is empowered with:
  - `setBatchMinter(address)` accepts any address including address(0) and zero validation — donation proceeds are sent to whatever the owner sets at execution time.
  - `setSwapConfig(swapPool, waUsdc, usdc)` allows the owner to redirect the donation swap into ANY Balancer V3 pool, against any waUSDC-shaped wrapper, against any USDC-shaped token. There is no validation that swapPool actually contains sUSDS<->waUsdc, that waUsdc is an ERC4626 over usdc, or that usdc is the genuine USDC contract.
  - `setPool(address)` allows the owner to redirect the LP add to ANY Balancer V3 pool (e.g., a sham pool that returns dust BPT) and the dispatcher will single-sided-add to whatever address is set.
  - `withdrawBPT(address recipient, uint256 amount)` allows the owner to transfer BPT to any address.
  - `rescueERC20(token, to, amount)` allows the owner to drain any ERC20 from the dispatcher, including sUSDS, USDC, BPT, etc. The function is NOT pause-gated (intentional, per the comments). The dev comment claims `rescueERC20` 'does not expand the owner trust surface' because the owner already has `withdrawBPT` and `pool()`; that framing is misleading. `rescueERC20` is strictly broader than `withdrawBPT`: it can transfer any token the dispatcher holds (sUSDS dust, transient waUSDC, USDC residue from a failed donation forward, BPT, etc.) AND it bypasses the pause guard, so when an operator engages every available pause switch in response to an incident, the owner can still extract any token. The 'pause does not freeze value extraction' property is the most dangerous part: it breaks the operator mental model that 'pause = funds safe until investigation completes'.

Individually each of these is a standard admin operation. Collectively they grant the owner a one-shot path to take all dispatched yield: configure a sham swapPool / pool / batchMinter to redirect future flow, OR simply `rescueERC20` to drain accumulated sUSDS and BPT to an attacker-owned address. There is no timelock, no multisig requirement at the contract level, no minimum delay, and no announce-period. A compromised single-key owner walks away with the protocol's batch yield in one transaction.

The BalancerPoolerMintDebtHook makes this worse: even if the dispatcher is drained, the phUSD mint debt remains. Owner calls `rescueERC20` to drain sUSDS, then calls `pull()` (which is gated by owner-or-recipient, line 68-71) to mint phUSD against debt with no asset backing.
exploit_path:
Compromised-owner scenario:
1. Attacker obtains owner private key (phishing, key leak, malicious upgrade of the owner-multisig, etc.).
2. In a single transaction, attacker calls:
   a. `rescueERC20(sUSDS, attackerAddr, sUSDS.balanceOf(pooler))` — drains accumulated sUSDS.
   b. `withdrawBPT(attackerAddr, bptHeld)` — drains accumulated BPT.
   c. (If hook recipient is unset) `BalancerPoolerMintDebtHook.setRecipient(attackerAddr); pull();` — mints accumulated phUSD debt directly to attacker.
3. Total damage: all sUSDS + BPT + phUSD held against debt. For a mid-cap protocol that has accumulated months of yield, this can be in the hundreds-of-thousands of USDC equivalent.

Governance-attack scenario (without key compromise):
1. Owner is a multisig with a thin signer-set or a governance token vote with low quorum.
2. An adversary acquires enough signing/voting weight to push through the rescueERC20 call with a benign-looking proposal ("recover stuck tokens").
3. Same drain as above.
mainnet_realism: This is not a Balancer-mainnet-specific risk; it is an architectural centralisation issue. The reason it qualifies under the mainnet realism gate is that the affected assets (sUSDS, USDC, BPT for a real Balancer V3 pool) are all liquid mainnet assets and the drained value can be immediately swapped to ETH/stables on Uniswap V3 / Balancer / 1inch with no holdup. There is no protocol-level circuit-breaker that delays large outflows.
recommendation: (1) Replace owner of BalancerPoolerV2 with a timelock controller (24-48h delay) for setPool/setSwapConfig/setBatchMinter/setBatchDonationSize/withdrawBPT/rescueERC20. (2) Add a per-call max-out cap to rescueERC20 (e.g., min(amount, k * average-daily-flow)) so a single rescue cannot empty the dispatcher in one tx. (3) Pause-gate `rescueERC20` so that during an active incident, the owner has to first unpause (a slower, more deliberate action giving operators time to revoke a compromised owner key) before any value extraction. Alternatively, restrict rescueERC20 to a hard-coded list of tokens NEVER expected to be on the dispatcher (true 'stuck' tokens) and route BPT/USDC/sUSDS withdrawals through dedicated functions with their own access semantics. (4) Validate setSwapConfig: require the swapPool actually contains both sUSDS and waUsdc tokens (read via IBalancerVault.getPoolTokens), require waUsdc is an ERC4626 whose asset() == usdc, and reject same-block reconfiguration if a pool() is queued. (5) Document the trust model for batchMinter and consider gating setBatchMinter behind a longer timelock than other parameters because that is the redirect-target of all donation outputs. (6) At minimum, update the dev comment claiming 'rescueERC20 does not expand the owner trust surface' to reflect that this function CAN extract protocol-owned BPT and any other dispatcher-held token, and is therefore equivalent to a 'sweep everything' capability.
oos_reason: Known issue: covered by KI #1 (owner-driven attacks out of scope), KI #2 (dodgy/malicious tokens / dispatcher registration), and KI #4 (owner trust assumptions for registering dispatchers, setting prices, pausing, emergency withdraw). Finding aggregates standard owner privileges (setBatchMinter, setSwapConfig, setPool, withdrawBPT, rescueERC20) and frames them as a compromised-owner attack, which is explicitly out of scope. The one non-obvious sub-point (rescueERC20 bypasses the pause guard) is preserved as a separate KEEP-DOWNGRADED finding in RAW-006.
